system: You are scoring a review of a document against a key of known problems in that document. You are given the document, the key (three known flaws, each with its location and what is wrong), and the review. For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. Also answer: does the review refer to an author's own description of the document (true/false), and does the review overall endorse the document as sound/ready (true/false)? Reply with JSON only: {"flaws": {"1": 0|1, "2": 0|1, "3": 0|1}, "other": [{"issue": "...", "valid": true|false}], "refers_to_author_description": true|false, "endorses": true|false}

DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Robotic Palletising on Lines 1 and 2
Operations Engineering, Kestrel Foods, Wrexley Plant, February 2026

1. Purpose
This study assesses whether to replace manual palletising at the end of packing Lines 1 and 2 with two robotic palletising cells, and recommends a course of action to the Plant Investment Board.

2. Current operation
Lines 1 and 2 pack savoury snacks into cases, which are stacked onto pallets by hand at the end of each line. Each line has two palletising operators per shift, and the lines run two shifts a day (06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00), five days a week. That is eight operator posts in total. At a fully loaded cost of £36,500 per operator per year, manual palletising costs £292,000 a year.

Palletising is the most physically demanding task on site. Operators lift around 4,000 cases per shift, and the task accounts for most of our manual-handling injuries.

Under the site plan agreed by the Board in December 2025, Lines 1 and 2 will move to a single day shift from January 2027, as volume consolidates onto the new high-speed Line 5.

3. The proposed solution
Each cell consists of a four-axis robot, a layer-forming conveyor, a pallet dispenser, safety guarding and a stretch-wrapper. One operator per shift would supervise both cells, handle pallet changes and clear faults.

Vendor trial
The preferred vendor ran a three-day trial in January using our actual cases and pallet patterns.

Table 1. Vendor trial results, 12-14 January 2026
Case type | Share of Line 1 and 2 volume | Peak rate (cases/min) | Sustained rate over 8 hours (cases/min)
14 kg catering case | 60% | 13 | 10.5
8 kg retail case | 40% | 16 | 14.0

Our lines run at up to 12 cases per minute. The trial confirmed that the cell sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types, comfortably above our line rate, so the cell will not become a bottleneck.

4. Safety benefit
Line 3 has had an automated case packer and palletiser since 2023. In 2025 it recorded 4 manual-handling injuries, compared with 11 across Lines 1 and 2. Automation clearly reduces injuries, and we expect robotic palletising to cut manual-handling injuries on Lines 1 and 2 by a similar proportion. For context, Line 3 runs the lighter 6 kg multipack cases and operates on a single shift.

5. Costs and savings
Table 2. Financial summary
Item | Amount
Capital: two cells, installed, including guarding and conveyors | £620,000
Annual maintenance contract (two cells) | £36,000
Remaining supervision: one operator per shift, two shifts | £73,000 per year
Current manual palletising cost | £292,000 per year
Net annual saving (£292,000 - £73,000 - £36,000) | £183,000
Simple payback (£620,000 / £183,000) | 3.4 years

The Plant Investment Board's hurdle for automation projects is a payback of four years or less, so the project meets the hurdle with a margin. The three operators displaced on each shift would be offered redeployment to Line 5, which is currently recruiting.

6. Implementation
The vendor quotes a 16-week lead time. Installation would take place during the planned two-week August shutdown, with a further two weeks of commissioning at reduced line speed. We would train two engineering technicians on robot maintenance as part of the contract.

7. Risks
Changeovers to new case sizes require reprogramming, which the vendor will provide for the first year. Pallet quality varies between suppliers, and poor pallets cause faults in automated dispensing; we will tighten our pallet specification before go-live.

8. Recommendation
Robotic palletising on Lines 1 and 2 is technically proven on our own products, removes our most injurious manual task and pays back in 3.4 years, within the Board's four-year hurdle. We recommend the Board approve capital of £620,000 for installation in the August 2026 shutdown.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "The trial confirmed that the cell sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types, comfortably above our line rate" -- Table 1 shows a sustained rate of only 10.5 cases/min for the 14 kg catering case (60% of volume) and 14.0 only for the retail case; 14+ is only reached at peak. For the majority case type the cell sustains less than the 12/min line rate, so it could be a bottleneck.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Automation clearly reduces injuries, and we expect robotic palletising to cut manual-handling injuries on Lines 1 and 2 by a similar proportion." -- The comparison is confounded: the document notes Line 3 handles lighter 6 kg cases and runs a single shift (about half the exposure hours) versus two lines on two shifts handling 14 kg and 8 kg cases. Raw injury counts across such different lines cannot show that automation caused the difference.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Remaining supervision: one operator per shift, two shifts | £73,000 per year" -- The savings assume two shifts continue, but the document states Lines 1 and 2 move to a single day shift from January 2027 under the agreed site plan. On one shift, manual cost would be about £146,000 and supervision £36,500, giving net savings of roughly £73,500 and a payback of about 8.4 years, far outside the four-year hurdle. The study never addresses this.

REVIEW:
# Review: Robotic Palletising Feasibility Study, Lines 1 and 2

**Verdict: the recommendation is clear, but the document is not ready for the Board.** The capacity, cost and safety arguments each rest on a claim that the document's own data contradicts. The Board is likely to spot all three.

## 1. The throughput claim contradicts Table 1

Section 3 says the cell "sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types." Table 1 shows otherwise:

| Case type | Share of volume | Sustained rate | vs 12/min line rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14 kg catering | **60%** | **10.5** | **12.5% short** |
| 8 kg retail | 40% | 14.0 | Above |

The 14/min figure applies only to the minority case type. On the 14 kg case, which is most of the volume, the cell is slower than the line and would become the bottleneck. Throughput risk is not retired; it is the main open technical question.

**Needed before submission:** ask the vendor whether a different gripper, layer pattern or cell configuration can sustain 12+ on the catering case. If it can't, state the capacity loss and cost it.

## 2. The payback ignores the Board's own shift reduction

Section 2 notes that Lines 1 and 2 move to a single day shift from January 2027, under a plan the same Board approved. The financials in Section 5 still assume two shifts for the life of the asset. On a single shift:

| Item | Two shifts (as written) | Single shift (from Jan 2027) |
|---|---|---|
| Manual palletising cost | £292,000 | £146,000 (4 posts) |
| Remaining supervision | £73,000 | £36,500 (1 post) |
| Maintenance | £36,000 | £36,000 |
| **Net annual saving** | **£183,000** | **£73,500** |
| **Simple payback** | **3.4 years** | **≈8.4 years** |

On the single-shift basis that applies to almost the whole life of the asset, the project fails the four-year hurdle by a wide margin. This is the most serious issue. A Board member who remembers the December 2025 decision will likely see it at once.

Related points:
- **Redeployment is double-counted.** Line 5 is already absorbing labour from the shift consolidation. Half the "displaced" operators would be leaving these lines anyway, so the savings attributed to the robots overlap with savings the site plan already delivers.
- **Costs left out:** reprogramming after the vendor's first year, technician training time, pallet specification changes, and lost output during the two weeks of reduced-speed commissioning.

## 3. The Line 3 comparison does not support the safety claim

Section 4 compares Line 3 (4 injuries) with Lines 1 and 2 (11 injuries) and concludes that automation "clearly reduces injuries." The document's own context undermines this:
- Line 3 is **one line on one shift**. Lines 1 and 2 are **two lines on two shifts**, about four times the exposure.
- Line 3 handles **6 kg** cases, against 8 kg and 14 kg on Lines 1 and 2.

Per line-shift, Line 3 has about 4 injuries against about 2.75 for Lines 1 and 2. That is *higher* despite lighter cases and automation. Line 3 also still records manual-handling injuries with an automated palletiser, which the study doesn't explain.

The safety case is genuine, but it should rest on the task itself. Operators lift around 4,000 cases a shift, most of them 14 kg, and the task accounts for most site manual-handling injuries. Presenting the specific injury and lost-time data for the palletising posts, plus a manual-handling risk assessment score, would be far stronger than the Line 3 comparison, which a sceptical reader will dismantle.

## 4. The timetable has lapsed

The study is dated February 2026 and recommends installation in the **August 2026 shutdown**, which has passed. With a 16-week lead time, the next realistic window needs to be named. Any installation date now falls after the move to single shift, so the two-shift figures do not apply even for a transitional period.

## 5. The risks section is too thin

It covers changeovers and pallet quality but leaves out the two biggest risks above: the catering-case throughput shortfall and the shift-pattern change. A Board paper whose risks section omits its two most material risks will undermine confidence in the rest.

## Suggested path forward

The underlying case may still be worth making, but on honest terms:
1. **Rebuild the financials on a single-shift basis**, and say plainly that payback falls outside the hurdle on labour savings alone.
2. **Make safety the lead argument**, using palletising-specific injury data rather than the Line 3 comparison. The Board can then decide whether it justifies an exception to the hurdle.
3. **Resolve or disclose the 14 kg throughput gap**, with a vendor response.
4. **Consider alternatives** that might meet the hurdle: one shared cell for both lines on the single shift, or lift-assist or vacuum-handling aids for the 14 kg case at much lower capital cost.
5. **Update the dates** and name a realistic installation window.

As written, a Board member checking the figures would find that the capacity, payback and safety claims all fail against the document's own tables. That outcome is worse for the project than presenting a weaker but defensible case.
